Younger people don't believe me, but there was a time when you couldn't choose when to watch a series. If the new episode was on Thursday at eight, you had to be at home, in front of the TV, at eight. No pause, no rewind. And the next day, everybody would talk about it at work or at school. Did you see what Ross did? Can you believe it? We used to wait a whole week for the next episode. Today, of course, it's much easier. But I miss one thing. We used to watch the same thing at the same time as everybody else. It made us feel connected.

Nostalgia used to be seen as a problem, almost an illness. Today we know it's much more positive than that. It's a mix of happiness and a little sadness when we think about the past. Research shows that people feel more nostalgia when they're stressed, lonely, or going through a big change. That's when we go back to the old songs and the old series. And it actually helps. When we look back on good moments, we feel more connected to other people and less alone. So if you rewatch the same sitcom after a hard week, don't feel guilty. Your brain knows what it's doing.

I grew up in a small town in Australia, and every afternoon after school, I used to watch reruns of an American sitcom. My mum thought I was wasting my time. But I would repeat the lines with the characters, and I would write the best jokes in a notebook. Without noticing, I was learning how Americans really speak. Years later, when I visited New York for the first time, I was surprised. People really talked like the characters in the show! I didn't use to think TV could teach you anything. Now I'm used to recommending it to everybody who's learning English.
